clinicalPearls: A benign but locally aggressive sellar/suprasellar tumour arising from remnants of Rathke's pouch along the craniopharyngeal duct
Shows a bimodal age distribution, with the adamantinomatous type predominating in children and a papillary type more typical in adults
Compression of the optic chiasm classically causes bitemporal visual field loss, while hypothalamic-pituitary involvement produces endocrine deficits
Growth hormone and gonadotrophin deficiencies are common; diabetes insipidus and other posterior pituitary problems may occur, particularly after surgery
The adamantinomatous variant characteristically shows cystic components, calcification and a mixed solid-cystic appearance on imaging
Cyst fluid is often described as machinery-oil-like, cholesterol-rich material at operation
Hypothalamic damage, whether from tumour or treatment, can lead to obesity, disordered temperature and thirst regulation, and behavioural change
Management balances surgical resection, often transsphenoidal or transcranial, with radiotherapy and long-term hormone replacement to preserve function
reference.pathophysiology: Craniopharyngiomas develop from epithelial remnants of the craniopharyngeal duct and Rathke's pouch in the sellar and suprasellar region. Although histologically benign, they enlarge and encroach on adjacent structures, compressing the optic chiasm, pituitary gland and stalk, hypothalamus and third ventricle. The adamantinomatous subtype, linked to Wnt/beta-catenin pathway activation, tends to be cystic and calcified, whereas the papillary subtype, associated with BRAF mutation, is usually solid. Mass effect and infiltration produce the visual, endocrine and hydrocephalic manifestations, and hypothalamic disruption underlies the metabolic and regulatory sequelae.
additionalDifferentials: Germ cell tumour of the suprasellar region
additionalInvestigations: Magnetic resonance imaging of the pituitary and hypothalamic region
Formal visual acuity and visual field assessment
Assessment of posterior pituitary function including for diabetes insipidus
Histological and molecular characterisation of resected tissue
redFlags: Rapidly progressive visual loss from chiasmal compression
Raised intracranial pressure or obstructive hydrocephalus
Hypothalamic dysfunction with disturbed thirst, temperature or consciousness
reference.prognosis: Overall survival is generally good given the benign histology, but recurrence is frequent and long-term morbidity from hypopituitarism, visual impairment and hypothalamic obesity substantially affects quality of life, so lifelong endocrine and ophthalmic follow-up is required.
pitfalls: Mistaking a cystic calcified suprasellar mass for a simple pituitary adenoma
Failing to assess and monitor visual fields before and after treatment
Overlooking cortisol deficiency before surgery or before starting thyroid replacement
Underestimating the risk of postoperative diabetes insipidus and hypothalamic obesity
Assuming complete cure after resection despite a high recurrence rate
management: Surgical resection by transsphenoidal or transcranial approach as primary treatment, aiming to relieve mass effect while limiting hypothalamic injury
Radiotherapy, including stereotactic or proton techniques, for residual or recurrent tumour or as an alternative to aggressive resection
Cyst management with drainage or a reservoir device and intracystic therapy such as bleomycin or interferon for predominantly cystic tumours
Full hormone replacement for hypopituitarism, including glucocorticoid, thyroid hormone, sex steroids and growth hormone as required
Desmopressin for diabetes insipidus with careful perioperative fluid and electrolyte management
Consider BRAF and MEK-targeted therapy for papillary BRAF-mutant craniopharyngioma
Manage hypothalamic obesity and metabolic sequelae with dietetic and endocrine input
Provide lifelong endocrine and ophthalmological follow-up with MRI surveillance for recurrence
